newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WWF say sharks face extinction, monitoring urged.
newsitem.headline: WWF say sharks face extinction, monitoring urged.

text.p: International wildlife protection bodies said on Wednesday sharks of all species faced a growing threat of extinction and called for closer monitoring of shark fishing and trade in shark products.

The Swiss-based Worldwide Fund for Nature (WWF) urged the United Nations Food and Agricultural Organisation (FAO), whose Fisheries Committee meets in Rome next week, "to take emergency action before it is too late for sharks."

WWF said the Rome meeting, which has been called to examine the state of the world's fish stocks, would be presented with reports calling for urgent measures by governments and international organisations.

The reports were compiled by TRAFFIC International, the wildlife trade monitoring agency run jointly by the WWF and the also Swiss-based World Conservation Union, and the Washington Centre for Marine Conservation.

"WWF is becoming increasingly alarmed about the state of sharks around the world," said Michael Sutton, director of WWF's Endangered Seas Campaign. "Sharks are extremely vulnerable to overfishing," he declared.
"Shark fishing amounts to open season on the high seas, because very few shark fisheries are subject to any form of management by national or international authorities."
TRAFFIC's Executive Director Steven Broad said the body's research showed a highly active trade in sharks and shark products around the globe.
"However, both the fisheries and the trade are so poorly monitored that shark stocks could be seriously depleted in some areas before management needs can be identified," he said.
"Specific and accurate reporting of shark landings and trade would be a crucial first step to provide future security for shark populations."
WWF said that although FAO member countries reported a record high shark landing total of 730,000 tonnes in 1994, the actual catch volume was probably much higher.

The main shark fishing countries included Argentina, Brazil, Britain, France, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, the Maldives, Mexico, New Zealand, Pakistan, Portugal, South Korea, Spain, Sri Lanka, Taiwan and the United States, it added.
